The Quiet Return of the Night Train

By Ana Petrović

For decades the overnight sleeper looked like a relic. Budget airlines undercut it on price, high-speed rail undercut it on time, and operators quietly retired carriages that had crossed the continent since the nineteen-seventies. ARTICLE-START-MARKER

That story has reversed. Over the past five years more than a dozen new overnight routes have opened, linking capitals that had not seen a direct night service in a generation. Operators report that cabins on the most popular routes sell out weeks in advance, even at prices that compare poorly with a short flight.

Why travellers are coming back

Passengers give a mix of reasons. Some point to the climate cost of flying, others to the simple appeal of falling asleep in one city and waking up in another without the queues, security checks and transfers that bracket even a short flight. Business travellers like arriving in the city centre with a full working day ahead of them.

Rolling stock remains the bottleneck. New sleeper carriages take years to design, certify and build, and only a handful of manufacturers still make them. Several operators have refurbished decades-old cars as a stopgap while they wait for new fleets.

Timetabling is the other headache. Night trains share tracks with freight that also runs overnight, and maintenance crews do most of their work in the same hours. Every new route is a negotiation between infrastructure managers in each country it crosses.

Still, the momentum is real. If the new fleets arrive on schedule, the network of the late twenty-twenties could rival the one that was dismantled at the turn of the century. ARTICLE-END-MARKER
